title: Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ tó gbó kò ní kùkùté nínú; àgbà tó mọ̀wà kò ní kùsà. (Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ soup that is thoroughly cooked has no coarse lumps; an elder endowed with noble character possesses no crude flaws: Refinement in character mirrors perfection in culinary skill.)

Bí a bá ń jẹ ẹ̀bùn, a kì í fi ẹ̀rù ṣọ́ọ̀rọ̀; bí Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ bá wọ Àmàlà, àyà a balẹ̀. (When enjoying a blessing, one does not tremble in terror; when Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ embraces Àmàlà, peace and tranquil satisfaction descend upon the heart: True nourishment brings inner calm.)

Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ kò ní egungun, ṣùgbọ́n ó ń gbé amàlà mì. (Gbẹ̀gị̀rị́ possesses no rigid bones, yet it smoothly guides and swallows amàlà: Sovereign potency and enduring influence triumph through gentle persuasion rather than harsh confrontation.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas from the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the British Protectorate. London: Routledge; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ Spectacle. Seattle: University of Washington Press.

title: Abula
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àbùlà kì í ṣe àkúnya, ó ń jọ́ra bíi ọ̀pọ̀ èrò (Abula is not a solitary substance; it weaves together in the manner of many distinct thoughts: Unity emerges from harmonious multiplicity.)

Gbègìrì ń ṣe ara rẹ̀ ní pọ́n-ọ́n, ewédú ń fa kọ́lá-kọ́lá, àbùlà la fi ń kẹ́ amàlà lẹ́wà (Gbegiri maintains its radiant golden glow, ewedu draws its slippery emerald sheen, and together as Abula they adorn the amala with majesty: Collaboration creates an elegance unattainable in isolation.)

Àbùlà kò ṣòro jẹ, àti-pèsè rẹ̀ ló gba ọgbọ́n. (Àbùlà is effortless to consume, but orchestrating its tripartite harmony requires supreme wisdom: True collective synergy demands mastery of diverse elements.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas from the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the British Protectorate. London: Routledge; Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan: Ibadan University Press.

title: Ẹ̀fọ́ Rírò
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹ̀fọ́ tí a fi epo rò kì í bàjẹ́; àbùkù kọ́ ní ń bọ́ sí orí ẹni rere. (Leafy greens properly stirred with abundant palm oil never spoil easily; ignominy never falls upon the head of the virtuous: Diligent preparation protects moral integrity.)

Bí ẹ̀fọ́ kéré lójú ọbẹ̀, a kì í fọwọ́ rọ́ ọ sẹ́gbẹ̀ẹ́; ohun tí a bá fi sùúrù rò ní ń kún inú afẹ́fẹ́. (Though the greens seem modest in the pot, one does not dismiss them disdainfully; whatever is stirred with enduring patience spreads fragrant abundance.)

Ẹ̀fọ́ tí a kò fi ata àti epo si, a kì í pè é ní ẹ̀fọ́ rírò. (Greens cooked without rich pepper and red palm oil cannot be deemed true stirred greens: Genuine enterprise demands full commitment rather than half-hearted effort.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society. São Paulo: Odebrecht; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas from the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the British Protectorate. title: Èwùrà
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Èwùrà ń fẹ́ gbẹ́jẹ̀ nínú odó, a kì í fẹ́ fún un ní ààyè (The water yam seeks to liquefy and scatter within the mortar, yet the wise cook grants it no such license: Softness of character requires firm, measured discipline.)

Bí iṣu bá ta èwùrà, a kì í fi kọ́kọ́ kọ̀ ọ́ (Even when the harvested yam turns out to be water yam, one does not immediately reject it: True discernment perceives inherent value beneath fragile exterior.)

Bí èwùrà bá fẹ́ jẹ oyè iṣu funfun, yóò kọ́kọ́ fi ara balẹ̀ nínú odó. (If the water yam aspires to the noble title of white yam, it must first endure the trial of the mortar: Ambition without endurance yields only disappointment.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society. São Paulo: Odebrecht; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas from the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the British Protectorate. London: Routledge.

title: Ikọkọrẹ
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ikọkọrẹ kì í ṣe oúnjẹ àkànṣe fún olóye lásán, àmì ìrẹpọ̀ Ìjẹ̀bú ni (Ikọkọrẹ is not merely a delicacy for nobility; it is the enduring culinary symbol of Ìjẹ̀bú solidarity and communal harmony.)

Bí a bá ń jẹ ikọkọrẹ, a kì í ka ẹja t’ó wọ̀ ọ́ (When partaking of rich ikọkọrẹ pottage, one does not count the multitude of dried fish and seafood embedded within: Generosity must be bountiful and without petty reckoning.)

Ikọkọrẹ Ìjẹ̀bú kò gbọ́dọ̀ dọ́mi, oúnjẹ ọlọ́lá ló ń fẹ́ àbójútó. (The authentic Ikọkọrẹ of Ìjẹ̀bú must never be diluted with excess water; an aristocratic dish demands meticulous custody: True cultural heritage tolerates no compromises in standards.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas from the Earliest Times to the Beginning of the British Protectorate. London: Routledge; Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan: Ibadan University Press.

title: Ẹ̀wà Àgányìn
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹ̀wà tí a bá fi sùúrù bọ̀, yóò dọ̀rọ̀ bí oyin (Beans boiled with steadfast patience inevitably become as luscious as honey: Enduring hardship sweetens the final reward.)
Àgányìn kì í bẹ́rù epo, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni kì í bẹ́rù iná (The master cook of Àgányìn fears neither boiling red palm oil nor blazing fire: Authentic mastery braves transformative intensity.)

Ẹ̀wà Àgányìn tí kò lẹ́po pupa dídùn, kì í dùn mọ́ ẹlẹ́nu. (Ẹ̀wà Àgányìn that lacks its deeply caramelized red palm-oil sauce brings no relish to the palate: Substance without seasoned character fails to inspire the spirit.)

title: Àádùn
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àádùn kì í ṣe oúnjẹ àṣán, àmì ayọ̀ àti ìbùkún ni. (Àádùn is never mere sustenance; it is the physical herald of joy and covenantal blessing: Sacred sweetness seals auspicious alliances.)
Bí a bá ń jẹ àádùn, a kì í fojú kan ilẹ̀ wò pẹ̀lú ìbànújẹ́. (When one partakes of sacred àádùn, one's eyes must not stare at the earth in sorrow: Divine sweetness demands gladness of heart.)

Àádùn tútù kì í kùnà lójú àlejò; ẹbọ ayọ̀ la fi ń kẹ́ ènìyàn. (Freshly spiced corn confectionery never fails before an honored guest; joy is the offering with which we honor humanity: Sharing auspicious gifts banishes bitter discord.)
provenance_and_citations: Bascom, William (1951). Yoruba Food and Cooking. Africa: Journal of the International African Institute, 21(1), 41–53; Verger, Pierre Fatumbi (1995).
